summary: Sol a Sol is a browser game in Scratch where kids aged 7–12 keep a Mars outpost alive for 5 sols (Mars days) by balancing three resources: energy, air and shield. Every decision has a visible cost before the player chooses, and some costs arrive the next day, like leaving solar panels out during a dust storm. Real NASA data drives the risk: solar particle clouds come from NASA DONKI with their real date and speed, and faster clouds cost more shielding. Players explore outside with a draining suit tank to collect ice (air), regolith (shield) and dusty panels (energy), and at night they decide whether to spend energy on greenhouse lights to grow lettuce, as NASA's Veggie experiment does. Real Mars sounds recorded by Perseverance play outside. The game is bilingual (Spanish/English), replayable, and failure is a lesson, not a punishment. It was play-tested by a team member in the target age range.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Sol a Sol teaches the real trade-offs of surviving on Mars through play. Each sol follows the same loop: (1) an event arrives: a dust storm, a real solar particle cloud, or a broken air recycler; (2) the player picks one of two options, each showing its cost as icons, so no choice is free; (3) the player decides whether to spend air to go outside; (4) outside, they collect resources while their suit tank drains; (5) a guide character, Lu, shares the real NASA fact behind the event; (6) at night, inside the greenhouse, the player decides whether to spend energy on grow lights. Two lit nights give a lettuce harvest worth +2 air.

REAL NASA DATA

- NASA DONKI (CME service): 10 real coronal mass ejections from Sep–Nov 2026, embedded with date and speed. Clouds over 900 km/s cost more shield. The start screen shows recent space weather from DONKI. Data is archived and labeled as not live.

- Perseverance microphone recordings (NASA/JPL-Caltech): Martian wind, a dust devil and the rover driving, only trimmed and volume-adjusted.

- Facts behind each mechanic: the 2018 dust storm that ended Opportunity, the Mars–Earth signal delay (up to ~22 min), water ice found by Phoenix, regolith as radiation shielding, wind cleaning rover panels, and Veggie lettuce eaten on the ISS in 2015.

All sources are credited inside the game on a Sources screen.

DESIGN FOR AGES 7–12

Three resources only, shown as blocks like a phone battery. The base shows its state: windows go dark with low energy and plants wilt with low air. Terms are explained in context ("sol = Mars day"). Sol 1 is practice with no timer; later events give 10 seconds, like real crews deciding before help arrives. Events and resource positions are random, so every mission plays differently. When the mission fails, the guide names what ran out and invites another strategy.

HOW WE BUILT IT

Scratch 3 (browser, no download or account needed). The idea, challenge choice, every design decision and play-testing came from the team. A team member in the target age range tested each version, and her feedback shaped the game: a visible suit tank, a goal for exploring, an inside view of the greenhouse, simpler screens, a sound button and Spanish/English support.

USE OF AI
Visual design: Original hand-drawn sketches created by our team, vectorized into SVG with AI assistance (Claude). Code: Game logic and Scratch architecture designed, adjusted, and assembled by Team Galactica Recall, with AI assistance (Claude) for code generation and debugging. Project text: Drafted with AI and reviewed/edited by the team. Audio: UI sounds are from Scratch's built-in library; Mars sounds are real NASA recordings. The game displays a visible AI credit on screen, and a sketch-vs-final image documents our creative process. No NASA logos or branding were generated or used.

IMPACT

Kids walk away understanding that on Mars every watt, breath and shield has a cost, and that real space weather changes real risk.
